podcast.title: Formation (1984)
podcast.body: The Tragically Hip was formed in 1984 when Gord Downie reconnected with Rob Baker and Gord Sinclair at Queen's University. They recruited high school student Johnny Fay on drums and a more experienced saxophone player from British Columbia named Davis Manning. "This was 1984."

podcast.title: Formation and Name Origin (1984)
podcast.body: The Tragically Hip formed in 1984 in Kingston, Ontario, with Gord Downie (20 years old at the time), Gord Sinclair, Robbie Baker, Johnny Faye, and sax player Dave Manning (about 15 years older). They took their name from a skit in a 1981 VHS tape called "Elephant Parts," produced by video pioneer Michael Nesmith (formerly of The Monkees). The phrase "tragically hip" also appears in Elvis Costello's 1982 song "Town Cryer" from the "Imperial Bedroom" album. "Things started coming together in 1984 when Gord, then 20 years old, the other Gord, Robbie, Johnny Faye, and a sax player, about 15 years older than everyone named Dave Manning, formed the tragically hip, taking their name from a skit in a 1981 VHS tape making the rounds called Elephant Parts."

podcast.title: Lineup Change (1986)
podcast.body: In 1986, Davis Manning, the saxophone player who was about 15 years older than the other members and brought valuable experience, left the band. He was replaced by Paul Langua, who became the new rhythm guitarist and was noted for his skill in playing Rolling Stones songs, shifting the band's sound from saxophone-driven to more guitar-oriented. "In 1986, Manning left, and his replacement was Paul Langua. So instead of a saxophone player, the hip had a new rhythm guitarist, who was pretty good at playing some stone songs."

podcast.title: Lineup Change and Stability (1986)
podcast.body: In 1986, the same year Gord Downie graduated from Queens University, founding sax player Dave Manning left the band. He was replaced by Paul Langlois, who had first met Gord Downie in grade 11 and was the son of the school's gym teacher and football coach. With Langlois joining, the lineup of The Tragically Hip remained unchanged for the next 31 years. "In 1986, the same year Gord graduated from Queens with a bachelor's degree, Dave Manning bowed out of the band and he was replaced by Paul Langua, who first met Gord when they were both in grade 11."

podcast.title: Artwork for Fully Completely by Leav Prinz
podcast.body: Rob Baker, the band's art student, was tasked with overseeing album art. While on his honeymoon, he developed conceptual ideas for the cover, including themes of a "Dutch life cycle" encompassing decay, decadence, birth, and death, as well as a "back and alien feast." Discovering artist Leav Prinz in *Zoom* magazine, Baker was impressed by her technique of pressing objects like bodies, coins, fish, and fruit onto a laser copier to create images with perceived depth. He contacted Prinz, who then brought a sketch to London. The final album cover was created in Battery Studios over a weekend (Friday night through Sunday) using a laser copier, guided by Prinz's distinct artistic vision and unique technique. The artwork was considered a crucial step in defining the band's visual identity. "And she created this beautiful life-size piece of art. And I think at that point that I realized there was something really special going on."

"Sometimes he tell a story in the middle of the song, like the famous Killer Whale Tank tale. Sometimes Gord would just go off and start seeing another song."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Magnetic Tape Degradation and Baking Process
podcast.body: Magnetic tapes degrade over time, a process often indicated by an "acidic" or "vinegary" smell. To recover audio, these tapes must undergo a "baking" process, typically in a small oven (likened to an easy-bake oven) at a low temperature, such as 325 degrees for 30 minutes. This process aims to remove humidity and re-adhere the magnetic particles to the tape, allowing for a single transfer. The transfer must occur within a "12 hour period" after the tapes have cooled, as the effect is temporary. After their discovery, the *Saskadelvia* tapes were baked and digitized at Revolution studio in Toronto, with the band acknowledging the poor preservation of the originals. "if you lift the lid on it and it smells kind of acidic like vinaigrette, then you really have got like one go out and you've got to bake it."

"The hip got a big break when a friend gave a copy of their demos to Hugh Seagall, a friend and former senator in Ottawa. podcast.title: Master Tape Search and Recovery
podcast.body: The search for the *Road Apples* session tapes was an "archeological dig" involving multiple trips by Johnny Fay to Universal Music's storage. Of the estimated 65 reels of two-inch tape recorded, only about 20 were found initially, some labeled, while 25 reels are still missing. Subsequent batches were identified by matching the handwriting of engineer Bruce Barris on the spine of unlabeled boxes. The tapes were not archived systematically, being "spread all over the place" and sometimes mixed with recordings by other artists. This haphazard storage contributed to the two-year search. "it's been a really crazy process, almost two years in the making trunks, trying to track this record down."

podcast.title: Recording Delay for Fully Completely
podcast.body: The band's initial plans to record *Fully Completely* in April 1992 were delayed by four months. This postponement was due to the complexities involved in transitioning to a new producer, Chris Sangerides, and a different studio in a new country (Battery Studios in the UK). Despite the initial complications, this delay proved beneficial, allowing the band crucial time to refine songs written in late 1991, undertake a quick tour of Australia to road-test new material before tough audiences, and compose additional new songs. "The hip had planned to record it in April 1992 but something went wrong with the recording dates. They were moving to a different producer and to a different studio in a different country, so arrangements were a little more complicated and the recording dates had to be pushed back four months."

podcast.title: Recording Process for Fully Completely
podcast.body: The recording sessions for *Fully Completely* commenced at Battery Studios in North London on July 29, 1992. The initial four weeks were dedicated exclusively to recording bass and drums, with scratch guitars and vocals used only as guides for placement. The subsequent instrumental and vocal layers were recorded over two weeks, followed by another two weeks for mixing. This meticulous, layered approach, distinct from their previous live-style recordings, aimed to achieve a "bigger sound" with greater isolation for individual instruments, allowing for more specific treatment and resulting in more impactful guitar sounds. "When the sessions began on July 29th, 1992, the first four weeks were nothing but drums and bass."

podcast.title: Road Apples Album Title Origin
podcast.body: The original title proposed for the 1991 album was "Saskadelvia," a band inside joke derived from frequently touring and not knowing what town they were in. However, the US record company rejected it as "too Canadian." The band then chose "Road Apples," a term with multiple Canadian meanings: it refers to horse manure (hence the joke about calling their own album "horse shit" to preempt critics) and is also slang for road hockey, where a piece of frozen horse manure might be used as a puck in their parents' generation. For promotion, actual road apples were encased in Lucite and sent to various people. "Someone made the joke. Oh, I think we're in Saskadelvia. And we thought it was a funny title. And the record company, US record company, said, yeah, too Canadian. We can't do that."

podcast.title: Road Apples Recording Sessions
podcast.body: The *Road Apples* album was recorded at Kingsway Studios in New Orleans in September 1990. The band arrived with around a dozen songs but continued writing, ending up with "way more songs than they could use." Producer Don Smith's style involved extensive pre-production, meticulous microphone placement, and non-stop recording to "catch a vibe." This creative period, marked by the band ditching individual songwriting for collective effort, resulted in a surplus of tracks, some of which were left unreleased to pare the album down to a concise dozen songs and ensure diversity. "the start of a really creative period for us where we had kind of ditched the idea of individually writing and really starting to get our chops together, writing together, which is opening up huge."

podcast.title: US Market Struggles (1990s onward)
podcast.body: The Tragically Hip never achieved major stardom in the American market, a phenomenon that has become an area of study. While they have pockets of support, their timing often did not align with prevailing American rock trends. For instance, in the 1990s, American rock was dominated by grunge, then hip hop, and later indie rock (like The Strokes or The White Stripes), none of which perfectly matched the Hip's style. "Why has the tragically hip never been able to break through in the States? While this isn't entirely true, the hip do have pockets of support in America. But unlike Brian Adams or Lannis Morsehsett or Nickelback, it just seems that their timing was off. Their music was great, but whenever they were hot, American rock and roll attitudes were somewhere else. In the 90s, it was grunge, and the hip are not grunge. Then came hip hop. Hip didn't belong there. Then it was Indy Rock and the flavor of the strokes, so the white stripes and the hip didn't really fit in there either."

xref.title: Battle of Bands Win Led to Bob Rock's First Ever Production Credit
xref.body: The band started as the K-Tels in 1978 in Vancouver but were threatened with legal action by the cheap record company K-tel International and renamed themselves Young Canadians. Frontman Art Bergman would remain a presence in Canadian alt-rock for decades, ultimately being made a Member of the Order of Canada in 2020. The band won a local Battle of the Bands contest that awarded them studio time at a new facility called Little Mountain Sound. The engineer assigned to these unknown contest winners was a young man named Bob Rock — it was the first time Rock ever produced anything. He went on to produce Metallica, Mötley Crüe, Bon Jovi, The Cult, the Tragically Hip, and many others. "The engineer assigned to them was some kid named Bob Rock."

xref.title: Solo Career Motivation
xref.body: Despite The Tragically Hip's immense success, Gord Downie felt a creative need to pursue projects outside the band, leading to his solo career. "The hip was a great success but creatively this wasn't enough for Gord. He had things he wanted to do outside the band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Suicide and Legacy
xref.body: Jim Ellison, the singer for Material Issue, tragically committed suicide, which derailed the band's career. His life and music left a lasting impact, inspiring The Tragically Hip's song "Escape is at Hand for the Traveling Man" and being honored by the annual "International Pop Over Throw" festival in Chicago. "However, their spirit lives on. Chicago, host an annual festival called International Pop Over Throw that's been going on since 1997, and it features bands in the whole PowerPop vein."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: The Bathouse Recording Experience
xref.body: The band recorded their "Hope and Ruin" album at The Bathouse, The Tragically Hip's studio in Bath, Kingston. This studio is described as an old coach house with a swimming pool, basketball court, grand piano, and living/sleeping quarters upstairs, functioning as a live-work recording space. "It's one of these old-style live work recording studios."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: The Tragically Hip Connection
xref.body: The Trews opened for The Tragically Hip in 2004 and maintained contact with them, leading to Gord Sinclair producing "Hope and Ruin" at The Bathouse. The Bathouse also served as a "Hip museum," featuring artifacts like the console from "Phantom Power," a painting from "In Between Evolution," and original artwork from "Fully Completely." "getting to work in this like house that's technically a hip museum."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Trews: In Their Own Words

xref.title: Will to Tour
xref.body: Despite his severe health challenges and cognitive decline, Gord's incredible will drove him to insist that The Tragically Hip rehearse and tour in spring 2016, even though he couldn't remember song titles, albums, or lyrics. "Gord's will had to have been incredible because he recovered enough through the spring of 2016 to insist that the hip get back together and start rehearsing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Writing Room Collaboration
xref.body: Mark Fraccard, who was the front of house mixer for The Tragically Hip, shared a writing room in Toronto with Ian Thornley and Colin Cripps. "Mark Freakon. He was the front house mixer for the hip."
